Source: Hermann Jacobi's 1884 translation of the Kalpa Sutra's 'Life of Rishabha' section, fetched directly from the sacred-texts.com etext (part of Sacred Books of the East vol. 22, itself unambiguously public domain by age). The Kalpa Sutra narrates Rishabha's (Rishabhanatha's) life in the same formulaic template it uses for Mahavira and the other Jinas -- this manifest follows that same formal, repetitive scriptural register rather than smoothing it into modern narrative prose, to stay faithful to the source.

content.text: The Kalpa Sutra records that the Arhat Rishabha, the Kosalian, descended from heaven and took the form of an embryo in the womb of Marudevi, wife of the patriarch Nabhi, in Ikshvakubhumi. He belonged to the Kasyapa gotra, and had five names: Rishabha, First King, First Mendicant, First Jina, and First Tirthakara -- the first of the twenty-four Jinas whose lives the Kalpa Sutra records.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

content.text: As a king, Rishabha 'taught, for the benefit of the people, the seventy-two sciences, of which writing is the first, arithmetic the most important, and the knowledge of omens the last, the sixty-four accomplishments of women, the hundred arts, and the three occupations of men' -- establishing, in Jain tradition, the arts and civilization by which humankind first learned to sustain itself.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

content.text: Having ruled for millions of years, Rishabha 'anointed his hundred sons as kings, and gave each a kingdom.' Then, riding to the park called Siddhartha Vana and the tree Asoka, 'after fasting two and a half days without drinking water, [he] put on a divine robe, and together with four thousand of high, noble, royal persons, and Kshatriyas, he tore out his hair, and leaving the house entered the state of houselessness' -- renouncing his entire kingdom and family at the height of his power.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

content.text: The Kalpa Sutra records that 'the Arhat Rishabha, the Kosalian, for one thousand years neglected his body' in ascetic practice, meditating upon himself for a thousand years before attaining omniscience -- the longest recorded austerity of any of the twenty-four Jinas in the text.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

content.text: Outside the town of Purimatala, under the tree Nyagrodha, 'after fasting three and a half days without drinking water, being engaged in deep meditation,' Rishabha 'reached the infinite... highest knowledge and intuition called Kevala' -- omniscience -- becoming, in Jain tradition, the first being of this era to attain full liberation-knowledge and to teach it to others.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

content.text: The Kalpa Sutra records that Rishabha had eighty-four Ganas and eighty-four Ganadharas (chief disciples), and 'an excellent community of eighty-four thousand Shramanas with Rishabhasena at their head,' three hundred thousand nuns led by Brahmisundari, over three hundred thousand lay votaries led by Sreyamsa, and over five hundred thousand female lay votaries led by Subhadra -- among the largest monastic communities recorded of any Tirthakara in the text.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)

content.text: On the summit of Mount Ashtapada, in the company of ten thousand monks, 'after fasting six and a half days without drinking water,' Rishabha died and attained final liberation. The Kalpa Sutra closes his account with the words: 'End of the Life of Rishabha. End of the Lives of the Ginas [Jinas]' -- marking him as the first and, in this text's arrangement, the culminating figure among the lives of the Tirthakaras it records.
content.source_name: Jaina Sutras, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22), 'Kalpa Sutra: Life of Rishabha', translated by Hermann Jacobi (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884)
